```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(BUCSS)
# Helpers for numbers quoted in the text: one row of a result by its term, and
# a proportion at the printed tables' precision, without the leading zero.
row_value <- function(x, term) x$value[x$term == term]
apa <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  sub("^0\\.", ".", format(signif(x, digits), scientific = FALSE))
}
```

Two settings control how aggressively BUCSS corrects the prior study's effect:
`assurance` handles uncertainty, and `alpha_prior` handles publication bias.
This vignette explains what each one does and shows how the recommended sample
size responds as you turn each knob. The correction is described by Anderson,
Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and builds on the truncated noncentral distribution
of Taylor and Muller (1996).

## What Assurance Means Here

Assurance is the long run proportion of planned studies whose power reaches the
target. Imagine the prior study drawn again and again from its literature, each
draw seen only if it cleared the publication threshold that `alpha_prior`
describes, and a new study planned from each one. At the true effect, some of
those planned studies have at least the power you asked for and some fall
short; assurance is the proportion that reach it. If you plan for 80% power
with `assurance = .80`, about 80% of the studies planned this way have power of
at least 80%.

BUCSS delivers that proportion in a simple way. A planned study reaches its
target power whenever the noncentrality parameter it was planned from is at or
below the true one, because power rises with the effect (and, apart from
rounding the sample size up to a whole number and from the smallest sample size
a planner returns, the design's own minimum or the Welch planner's 10 per group,
only then). So BUCSS plans from the lower limit of a one-sided confidence interval for the prior study's
noncentrality parameter, at a confidence level equal to the assurance,
computed from the distribution of the prior statistic truncated at the
publication threshold: the value at which a published prior study would exceed
the observed statistic with probability `1 - assurance`, which Anderson,
Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) call the `1 - assurance` quantile of the likelihood
distribution. An interval at level .80 covers the true parameter in 80% of
repetitions, and in each of those repetitions the plan is large enough.

The term follows Kelley and Maxwell (2003), who used assurance in sample size
planning for the probability that a confidence interval will be no wider than
desired. Here it is the probability that the planned study's power will be at
least the desired power.

## Assurance: Correcting for Uncertainty

The value of `assurance` sets how much protection against uncertainty the plan
carries:

* `assurance = .5` selects the noncentrality parameter at which the observed
  statistic sits at the median of the publication-truncated distribution, a
  median unbiased estimate. This corrects for publication bias only; it does
  not add any cushion for uncertainty.
* `assurance > .5` selects instead a one-sided lower confidence bound at that
  level, which is a smaller, more conservative noncentrality parameter, and
  therefore a larger planned sample size. The extra sample size is the price of protecting against
  the chance that the prior estimate was lucky.
* `assurance < .5` is not recommended (the functions warn), because it implies
  under a 50% chance of reaching the desired power.

Why does uncertainty call for a larger sample at all? Suppose for a moment there
were no publication bias, so the reported effect were equally likely to fall
above or below the true value. The two kinds of error do not cancel, because the
sample size needed for a given level of power is a nonlinear function of the
effect size. An overestimate leads you to plan too small a study and cuts power
sharply, while an equally sized underestimate leads you to plan a larger study
and raises power by less. Averaged over the ways a noisy estimate can come out,
planning at face value loses more power than it gains, so protecting against
uncertainty means shifting the plan toward a larger sample. That is exactly what
assurance above .5 does.

Watch the recommended per-group sample size climb as assurance rises, for a
prior independent *t* test with *t* = 3.00 and 20 per group:

```{r}
assurances <- c(.5, .6, .7, .8, .9)
n_by_assurance <- sapply(assurances, function(a) {
  r <- ss_buc_independent_t(t_observed = 3, n = 20, assurance = a, desired_power = .80)
  r$value[r$term == "necessary_n_per_group"]
})
data.frame(assurance = assurances, necessary_n_per_group = n_by_assurance)
```

The climb is steep. A prior effect this uncertain calls for 130 per group at
80% assurance and over 5000 per group at 90%.

### When the Correction Cannot Be Made

Push assurance high enough on a weak or uncertain prior effect and the corrected
noncentrality parameter is driven to zero. That is the method telling you the
prior effect cannot be estimated with confidence at this level of assurance, so
sample size planning is not possible with these settings. The function stops
rather than returning a meaningless answer, and the error reports the largest
assurance the prior result can support so you know exactly how far to step back:

```{r eval = FALSE}
# Not run: this stops with an informative error.
ss_buc_independent_t(t_observed = 3, n = 20, assurance = .95, desired_power = .80)
#> Error: Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After
#> correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty
#> at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality
#> parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the
#> prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result
#> and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable
#> plan is about .90; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or
#> raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower
#> 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower
#> assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion
#> of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly.
#> 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it
#> is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's
#> literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias
#> to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's
#> journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a
#> more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no
#> publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and
#> Anderson and Kelley (2024).
```

That last sentence is worth dwelling on, because the first remedy looks
cheaper than it is. Assurance is a promise about the long run: at .90, nine
replications in ten reach your target power. If the prior result cannot
support .90 and you re-run at .80, the plan you get is a perfectly good .80
plan, but it is an .80 plan. You have not recovered the guarantee you wanted;
you have accepted a smaller one in exchange for a feasible study. Raising
`alpha_prior` is a different kind of move: it does not lower the guarantee,
it changes an assumption about the literature the prior study came from, and
it is defensible exactly to the extent that the assumption is.

The reported ceiling is exact: the largest assurance a prior result can support
is `1 - p/alpha_prior`, where *p* is the prior study's *p* value. Here that is
about .90, so .95 is out of reach but .90 or below is fine. The two remedies are
exactly the two knobs: lower the assurance to at or below the reported ceiling,
or assume less publication bias by raising `alpha_prior`, which lifts the
ceiling. When the ceiling is already at or below the .5 floor, only raising
`alpha_prior` can help.

Every successful call reports this same ceiling too, printed in the footer as
"Largest supportable assurance", so you can see how much headroom remains
before the correction breaks down. The printed result also gives the implied
total sample size for per-group and per-cell designs, saving you the
multiplication.

### The Ceiling, Drawn

The ceiling is easier to see than to read about, so `plot()` on any plan draws
it. The method re-runs that plan's own planner across a range of assurance
values and shows what happens on the way to the wall.

```{r ceiling-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.2, fig.alt = "Two panels sharing an assurance axis. On the left, the adjusted noncentrality parameter falls from about 2.6 to zero as assurance rises from .5 to the ceiling at .905. On the right, the necessary sample size per group climbs from 25 to tens of thousands on a logarithmic scale over the same range. Both panels shade the region beyond the ceiling and label it as one where no plan exists."}
plan <- ss_buc_independent_t(t_observed = 3, n = 20, assurance = .80)
plot(plan)
```

The point is the shape. Assurance does not degrade gracefully as it rises: it
hits a wall. On the left, the corrected noncentrality parameter, the quantity
the correction actually solves for, falls to zero. On the right, the sample
size that parameter implies grows asymptotically, and the vertical scale is
logarithmic because it spans three orders of magnitude over a range of
assurance a researcher might plausibly consider. The filled point is the plan itself, at
`assurance = .80`, and the shaded band is the region where the planner refuses.

That the sample size is finite everywhere left of the ceiling and undefined
everywhere right of it is not an artifact of the software. It is what the
prior result can and cannot support.

Read from the same figure, the two remedies in the error message are the two
things you can do to a wall. Lowering assurance moves the point left, along a
curve that is very steep near the ceiling, which is why a small step back can
buy a large reduction in sample size. Raising `alpha_prior` moves the wall
itself to the right.

The plotted values come back invisibly, so the figure can be redrawn with any
other graphics system (the call also draws the sample size panel again, which
is not repeated here):

```{r, fig.show = "hide"}
curve_values <- plot(plan, which = "size", n_points = 12)
head(curve_values, 4)
```

## alpha_prior: Modeling Publication Bias

`alpha_prior` is the significance level a prior result had to reach to be
published (more generally, to reach you): the correction assumes you see only
results with *p* below `alpha_prior`, and it undoes the selection that
assumption implies. Setting `alpha_prior = .05` assumes the field publishes
results with *p* < .05 and truncates the likelihood at that point. A larger
value assumes a more permissive literature and therefore less severe bias.

Setting `alpha_prior = 1` means there is no publication filter at all. Every
*p* value is at most 1, so any result would have been published whatever its
*p* value; there is then no publication bias to correct, and only the
correction for uncertainty, set by `assurance`, remains. That is appropriate
for a prior study that was never subject to the file drawer, such as a pilot
study. (BUCSS computes with .999 in place of exactly 1, as BUCSS 1.x did, so
plans match earlier versions; the section on safeguard power below shows that
the difference is negligible.)

A dissertation study is a similar case, since it is typically completed and
defended regardless of how the results turn out. Even a pilot study is not
guaranteed to be bias-free, though. If the researchers would have gone on to the
full study only after a promising pilot result, say *p* < .25, then the pilot
faced an informal filter of its own, and an `alpha_prior` between .05 and 1 may
describe it better than either extreme. An intermediate value above .05 also
suits a prior effect that was not the original study's focus, such as a
secondary effect reported alongside a study's main result, which usually faced a
weaker publication filter than the headline effect did.

Note that `alpha_prior` is not a confidence level and is distinct from
`alpha_planned`, which is the Type I error rate of the study you are designing.

Holding assurance at .80, watch the recommended sample size shrink as we assume
less publication bias:

```{r}
alphas <- c(.05, .10, .20, .50, 1)
n_by_alpha <- sapply(alphas, function(ap) {
  r <- ss_buc_independent_t(t_observed = 3, n = 20, alpha_prior = ap, assurance = .80,
                   desired_power = .80)
  r$value[r$term == "necessary_n_per_group"]
})
data.frame(alpha_prior = alphas, necessary_n_per_group = n_by_alpha)
```

Assuming the strongest bias (`alpha_prior = .05`) calls for 130 per group;
assuming none (`alpha_prior = 1`) calls for 37.

## Safeguard Power as a Special Case

Safeguard power (Perugini, Gallucci, & Costantini, 2014) is a way of planning
a new study from a prior study's effect size that guards against the prior
estimate being too large. Instead of planning for the effect size the prior
study observed, the researcher plans for the lower limit of a two-sided 60%
confidence interval around it, a limit that, in repeated sampling, falls below
the true effect 80% of the time. The new study then keeps its intended power
even if the true effect is somewhat smaller than the one observed. Safeguard
power allows for uncertainty in the prior estimate but not for publication
bias.

It is BUCSS with `alpha_prior = 1` and `assurance = .80`, that is, BUCSS
without the publication bias correction, at an assurance of .80, and seeing
why shows what each setting does.

* With `alpha_prior = 1` there is no publication filter, since no *p* value
  exceeds 1, so the truncation disappears and the truncated distribution of
  the prior statistic is its ordinary distribution. BUCSS computes with .999
  in place of exactly 1, as BUCSS 1.x did, so plans match earlier versions.
  That is a filter so lenient, dropping only results with *p* above .999, that
  it changes the plan negligibly; its size is given below.
* At `assurance = .80` the adjusted noncentrality parameter is then the value
  at which the observed statistic sits at the .80 quantile of that
  distribution: the lower limit of a one-sided 80% confidence interval, which
  is the lower limit of a two-sided 60% interval, since either way 20% is left
  below it.
* The plan is the smallest sample size whose ordinary power at that value
  reaches the target, which is what safeguard power prescribes.

For a paired *t* of 3.00 with 30 pairs, the lower limit of the 60% interval
can be found directly by inverting the noncentral *t* distribution, and the
ordinary power analysis at that limit gives the safeguard plan:

```{r safeguard}
t_obs <- 3
N <- 30
# The lower limit of a two-sided interval at confidence level C: the
# noncentrality parameter at which the observed t is the (1 + C)/2 quantile.
lower_limit <- function(C) {
  uniroot(function(ncp) pt(t_obs, df = N - 1, ncp = ncp) - (1 + C) / 2,
          c(0, 10), tol = 1e-10)$root
}
# Ordinary power of a paired t test with n pairs, at a noncentrality
# parameter stated for the prior study's N pairs.
power_at <- function(n, ncp) {
  crit <- qt(.975, df = n - 1)
  delta <- ncp * sqrt(n / N)
  (1 - pt(crit, df = n - 1, ncp = delta)) + pt(-crit, df = n - 1, ncp = delta)
}
safeguard_n <- function(ncp) {
  n <- 2
  while (power_at(n, ncp) < .80) n <- n + 1
  n
}
limit_60 <- lower_limit(.60)
plan_sg <- ss_buc_paired_t(t_observed = t_obs, N = N, alpha_prior = 1,
                           assurance = .80)
data.frame(method = c("safeguard power", "BUCSS, alpha_prior = 1"),
           ncp = c(limit_60, row_value(plan_sg, "ncp_adjusted")),
           necessary_N = c(safeguard_n(limit_60),
                           row_value(plan_sg, "necessary_N")))
```

In general, the lower limit of a two-sided interval at confidence level C is
`assurance = (1 + C)/2`: a 60% interval is assurance .80, an 80% interval is
.90, and a 90% interval is .95. The same prior shows the correspondence at
each level:

```{r safeguard-levels}
levels_C <- c(.60, .80, .90)
data.frame(
  confidence_level = levels_C,
  assurance = (1 + levels_C) / 2,
  interval_lower_limit = sapply(levels_C, lower_limit),
  ncp_adjusted = sapply(levels_C, function(C) {
    plan <- ss_buc_paired_t(t_observed = t_obs, N = N, alpha_prior = 1,
                            assurance = (1 + C) / 2)
    row_value(plan, "ncp_adjusted")
  }))
```

The differences that remain all make the BUCSS plan the same as the safeguard
plan or larger, never smaller. The first is the .999: a filter that hides only
results with *p* above .999 removes almost nothing, but it is not quite no
filter at all. The second applies to the *t* tests and to every effect on one
degree of freedom: BUCSS bounds the size of the effect whatever its sign, so
its interval is computed from the magnitude of *t*, where the signed interval
that safeguard power describes is computed from *t* itself. The difference is
the chance of a *t* at least as extreme in the opposite direction, which is
negligible for a convincing prior result and not for a weak one. For *F* and
chi square statistics on more than one degree of freedom there is no sign, and
the .999 is the only one of these two. Both lower the adjusted noncentrality
parameter, and both grow as the prior result weakens. At the safeguard
`assurance = .80`, as percentages of the parameter on the *F* and chi square
scale (on the *t* scale that the *t* planners report, each percentage is about
half as large), the .999 lowers it by 0.02% or less for a prior significant at
.01, by up to about 0.07% at the .05 threshold, by up to about 0.15% at .10,
and by about 0.3% at .15. The magnitude of *t* lowers it by less than 0.005% at
.01, by 0.3% to 0.7% at .05 (0.6% to 0.7% for a prior on 5 or more degrees of
freedom), by 6% to 7% at .10, and by about 30% at .15. A *t* test whose
two-sided *p* value is about .20 or more is declined by BUCSS at
`assurance = .80`, while the signed interval's lower limit stays above zero
until *p* reaches .40, with plans that run to thousands of participants.

The sample size a plan needs is close to inversely proportional to the
parameter on the *F* and chi square scale, so the plan grows by about the same
proportion before it is rounded up to a whole participant. The plan can
therefore equal the safeguard plan, be one or a few participants larger in a
plan of thousands even for a prior significant at .01 (7,825 pairs rather than
7,823 for a paired *t* significant at .01 with 3,000 pairs), be a few percent
larger in a very small plan (20 per group rather than 19 for an independent *t*
at the .05 threshold with 4 per group), or be much larger for a weak prior.
The same comparison for a prior of 30 pairs at several two-sided *p* values
shows the growth:

```{r safeguard-strength}
p_prior <- c(.01, .05, .10, .15)
t_prior <- qt(1 - p_prior / 2, df = N - 1)
signed_limit <- sapply(t_prior, function(t) {
  uniroot(function(ncp) pt(t, df = N - 1, ncp = ncp) - .80, c(0, 10),
          tol = 1e-10)$root
})
plans_1 <- lapply(t_prior, function(t) {
  ss_buc_paired_t(t_observed = t, N = N, alpha_prior = 1, assurance = .80)
})
data.frame(
  p_value = p_prior,
  signed_limit = signed_limit,
  ncp_adjusted = sapply(plans_1, row_value, term = "ncp_adjusted"),
  safeguard_N = sapply(signed_limit, safeguard_n),
  bucss_N = sapply(plans_1, row_value, term = "necessary_N"))
```

Two further differences can make the BUCSS plan larger. The first is that
BUCSS reads an unbalanced prior design as a balanced one. When only the prior
total is given and it does not divide evenly among the groups or cells, BUCSS
rounds the per-group or per-cell size both down and up and returns the larger
plan, which can make the plan larger by up to about the proportion that
rounding up adds to the prior size, less than 1/*n* for a prior study of about
*n* per group or cell, again before the plan is rounded up. When the
independent *t* planner is given two unequal group sizes, it reads the prior as
two groups of their harmonic mean, rounded down and up, on those balanced
designs' degrees of freedom rather than on the prior study's own (the two
sizes' sum less 2). The harmonic mean falls further below half the total the
more unequal the sizes, and fewer degrees of freedom lower the limit. For
similar sizes this adds little beyond the rounding, but for very unequal sizes
it can add much more, most when the harmonic mean is small. A *t* of 3.00 from
groups of 4 and 100, whose harmonic mean is 7.69, shows the difference:

```{r safeguard-unbalanced}
n_prior <- c(4, 100)
# Ordinary power of an independent t test with n per group at a standardized
# mean difference d.
power_ind <- function(n, d) {
  crit <- qt(.975, df = 2 * n - 2)
  delta <- d * sqrt(n / 2)
  (1 - pt(crit, df = 2 * n - 2, ncp = delta)) +
    pt(-crit, df = 2 * n - 2, ncp = delta)
}
# Safeguard power with the 60% limit read on 'df' and restated as a
# standardized mean difference by the factor 'to_d'.
safeguard_ind <- function(df, to_d) {
  limit <- uniroot(function(ncp) pt(3, df = df, ncp = ncp) - .80, c(0, 10),
                   tol = 1e-10)$root
  n <- 2
  while (power_ind(n, limit * to_d) < .80) n <- n + 1
  n
}
harmonic <- 2 * prod(n_prior) / sum(n_prior)
plan_unequal <- ss_buc_independent_t(t_observed = 3, n = n_prior,
                                     alpha_prior = 1, assurance = .80)
data.frame(
  prior_read_as = c("groups of 4 and 100, df 102", "7 per group, df 12",
                    "8 per group, df 14", "BUCSS, alpha_prior = 1"),
  necessary_n_per_group = c(
    safeguard_ind(sum(n_prior) - 2, sqrt(sum(1 / n_prior))),
    safeguard_ind(2 * floor(harmonic) - 2, sqrt(2 / floor(harmonic))),
    safeguard_ind(2 * ceiling(harmonic) - 2, sqrt(2 / ceiling(harmonic))),
    row_value(plan_unequal, "necessary_n_per_group")))
```

Safeguard power at the prior study's own design plans 15 per group. Read as
two groups of 7, which rounds the harmonic mean down and so favors a smaller
plan, the prior already plans 16 on its 12 degrees of freedom; read as two
groups of 8 on 14 degrees of freedom it plans 18, which is the BUCSS plan.

The second is the Welch planner's minimum of 10 per group, which can make its
plan larger. For the regression planners, the equivalence holds in the frame
`random_predictors` names: with sampled predictors, both the interval and the
power analysis use the distribution with random predictors.

With `alpha_prior` below 1, BUCSS applies the same construction to the
publication-truncated distribution, which is what the publication bias
correction adds to safeguard power; and with `assurance = .5` it plans from
the median unbiased estimate rather than from a lower limit.

## Seeing the Assurance Claim Exercised

Everything above is a claim about a long run that a user planning one study
never gets to watch. `ss_buc_sensitivity()` lets you watch it on your own
numbers. It reads the design and the planning inputs off a plan, simulates
prior studies of that design from a true effect you name, discards the ones a
literature would not have published, runs the same planner on each survivor,
and reports what happened.

You have to name the true effect; there is deliberately no default, because
defaulting to the corrected estimate would ask the method to grade its own
answer. The value goes on the same scale as the plan's own `ncp_adjusted`, so
that number is the natural anchor.

```{r}
plan <- ss_buc_paired_t(t_observed = 3, N = 30, assurance = .80)
ncp <- plan$value[plan$term == "ncp_adjusted"]
ncp
audit <- ss_buc_sensitivity(plan, true_ncp = ncp, replications = 2000,
                            seed = 2017)
audit
```

Two attainment rates are reported, and the gap between them is the point.
`attainment_with_refusals` lands on the requested assurance within simulation
error (here `r apa(row_value(audit, "attainment_with_refusals"))`, with a Monte
Carlo standard error of
`r apa(row_value(audit, "attainment_with_refusals_mcse"), 2)`), because that is
the quantity the guarantee is about: a refusal counts as attaining, since
declining to plan is the limiting case of an arbitrarily conservative plan.
`attainment` counts only the prior studies for which a plan was actually
issued, and it is lower, often much lower: here
`r apa(row_value(audit, "attainment"))` (Monte Carlo standard error
`r apa(row_value(audit, "attainment_mcse"), 2)`), because the method refuses
`r apa(row_value(audit, "refusal_rate"))` of the simulated published prior
results as too weak to plan from. That is what a user experiences, and it is
the visible price of a method that refuses rather than guesses. Its expected value is
`(assurance - refusal_rate)/(1 - refusal_rate)`.

The most useful thing to do with this function is to run it more than once,
at the corrected estimate and at values below it, and watch how fast the
attainment falls when the truth is smaller than the correction assumed. What
it cannot tell you is whether the distributional assumption behind a design is
right, since the simulation shares that assumption.

## Practical Guidance

* Make the corrections as minimal as you can defend. Each knob trades a modeling
  assumption for a smaller sample, and overstating either bias or uncertainty
  inflates the study unnecessarily.
* `assurance = .80` is a common, defensible choice. Reserve very high assurance
  for cases where a failed replication is especially costly, and expect the
  required sample size to grow quickly.
* Choose `alpha_prior` to reflect the publishing threshold in the prior study's
  field. Use `alpha_prior = 1` only when you genuinely believe the prior study
  escaped publication bias.
